Urban conflagration paper · national map

Where an urban conflagration is possible · 2026-10-15

Lower 48 states and DC · 126,333,967 building footprints (Microsoft, photos mostly 2014–21) · 38,455 blocks of more than 89 closely spaced buildings within 2.4 km of wildland, holding 7,160,150 buildings · hexagon map, wind-warning layer, state totals and a check against the ten known urban conflagrations

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-14 18:42 PDT

Every urban conflagration in the U.S. records since 2002 began where a fire reached a block of more than 89 closely spaced buildings, during a regional wind event. This map shows where the first condition is met within reach of wildland: 38,455 blocks, 5.7% of the country's buildings. It marks where an urban conflagration is possible, not where one is likely.Necessary-condition map: 35 m single-linkage components (≥ 90) of Microsoft v2 footprints ≥ 40 m², CONUS-wide (no tile or state cuts), with ≥ 1 member ≤ 2.4 km from NLCD 2019 wildland. Wind is a separate descriptive layer (NWS HW.W days, 2006–2025). Pre-registered (PA65).

How to read this page

What is marked. A block here is a chain of buildings, each with its centre within 35 m of the next (about a 20 m gap between walls). The paper found that no fire whose biggest such block held 89 or fewer buildings became an urban conflagration (0 of 338 fires in the USGS Carlson record 2002–22; 0 of 701 in our 2002–26 record; 0 of 431 CAL FIRE inspected incidents), while about 4 in 10 above that line did (10 of 25 in our record). The map marks blocks of more than 89 buildings with at least one building within 2.4 km of wildland.

What it is not. A necessary condition, not a forecast: most marked places have never burned and most never will. It says nothing about fire weather, building materials, defensible space or firefighting.

How this panel was checked
  • Only aggregates are drawn: hexagons of about 36 km²; no building or block outline.
  • Colour classes are counts of buildings; the hover gives the hexagon's total and share.
  • The wind layer is a separate tick box and never changes the hexagon colours.
  • Fire rings sit at the centre of each fire's largest destroyed chain.

Possible, not likely: fires that reached a big block within reach of wildland

In our 2002–26 record, 36 fires reached a big block within reach of wildland on this map, and 9 of them became urban conflagrations. Of the 718 fires that reached none, 1 did. The map marks where it can happen, not where it will.Exposed record buildings matched to the nearest Microsoft centroid ≤ 20 m; 'reached' = ≥ 1 match in a flagged component (D = 2.4 km). Vintage: share of matched footprints with capture date before ignition ≥ 0.5. Pre-registered as amendment 1 (labelled secondary) after the patch-level checks were seen.

  • Same national map for every fire; the fire's own exposed buildings decide 'reached'.

Check against the ten known urban conflagrations

The pre-registered bar (checks 1 and 2 pass for every event with photos from before the fire) is not met. Check 1 fails at Marshall 2021: its largest destroyed chain filled a block of 57, though the fire reached a block of 108 elsewhere. Check 2 fails at Sandalwood 2019, Glass 2020, Marshall 2021, where the map's blocks around the burned chain are smaller than in the fires' own lists. Check 3, which matches the paper's rule, passes for 9 of 10; the miss: Sandalwood 2019 (89 buildings on the map against 95 in its own list, 1 short).Rows: every (event, record) in fire_sig with LDC30 ≥ 50 (definition a0). Bar from prereg §4: all R-a pass and all R-b pass where matched footprints are mostly pre-ignition. Red boxes mark the failures that matter for the bar or the rule.

How this panel was checked
  • A necessary-condition check: it asks whether the map would have marked the places that burned, not whether it predicts fires.
  • Building photos: Sayre 2008, Tubbs 2017, Camp 2018 were photographed after the fire, so their burned blocks are missing or rebuilt; these rows say so and are not counted against the bar.
  • Microsoft lists footprints of at least 40 m²; the fires' own lists include smaller buildings, so the map's blocks can be smaller (Woolsey 2018: 152 on the map vs 153 in its own list; Sandalwood 2019: 89 on the map vs 95 in its own list; Glass 2020: 106 on the map vs 125 in its own list; Almeda Drive 2020: 330 on the map vs 414 in its own list).
  • Each event is shown in every record that holds it (17 rows for 10 events); no event is counted twice in the tiles.

How much the count depends on 'within reach of wildland'

The block rule alone marks 9,305,536 buildings (7.4% of all). Requiring wildland within 2.4 km (the reach used for 'indirectly exposed' buildings in the USGS Carlson record) keeps 77% of the blocks. Even at 100 m, 5,549 blocks remain: the count falls steadily as the distance shrinks, with no natural break, so the distance is a choice and is stated.Main rule pre-registered before any count (D = 2.4 km). Sensitivity: D ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1, 2.4, 5} km; SILVIS 2020 interface/intermix (per-building block class); WRC v2 BP > 0 at the building pixel; none. Shading: more = darker (no good/bad end).

How this panel was checked
  • One building layer (Microsoft footprints, imagery mostly 2014–21) and one block rule in every row; only the wildland rule changes.
  • Counts, not rates: the share column states its base (all mapped buildings).
  • Wildland distances are exact to 5 km (map tiles with a 5.1 km margin) and agree to the metre with an earlier independent calculation for all 92.5 million buildings within 1 km.
  • The distance was fixed before any count was seen; the other rows are reported, not chosen among.

The second condition, shown separately: how often damaging wind is warned for

55% of the buildings in big blocks within reach of wildland are in places with a High Wind Warning on at least one day a year on average. Every urban conflagration happened during a regional wind event, but warnings only partly capture those events: Diablo winds at Tubbs 2017 came with a Wind Advisory but no High Wind Warning.4452 of 4452 warned zone/county codes placed (outlines as issued, IEM shapefile export; retired codes included). Days = union of UTC days with an active HW.W across codes covering the H3 res-6 centre, ÷ 20 years. Not combined with the block flag.

How this panel was checked
  • Twenty full years, 2006–2025; the archive's partial 2005 and the partial 2026 are left out.
  • Warning rules differ between weather offices, so equal day counts do not mean equal winds everywhere.
  • Zone outlines are taken as issued, so warnings on zone codes the weather service has since retired are placed correctly.
  • Descriptive only: no combined risk score is made from wind and blocks.

Before using this map

  • Building photos are not current everywhere. Most footprints come from photos taken 2014–21. Places built since are missing; places burned and not yet rebuilt (Paradise, for example) are missing too.
  • Small buildings are left out. Footprints under 40 m² (sheds, small cabins) are not counted, so some blocks are smaller on the map than on the ground. Sandalwood 2019, a mobile-home park, counts 89 on the map against 95 in the fire's own list.
  • The line rests on few events. The 89 line rests on 10 urban conflagrations in three records (25 fires above the line in our record); re-estimated in each record it falls between 59 and 93 buildings.
  • Wildland is a land-cover class, and a generous one. Forest, shrub, grassland and wetland from the 2019 national land-cover map, not a fuel model; a patch a few hundred metres across counts, so city forest preserves and river woods do too. That is why Cook, IL and Cuyahoga, OH rank high among counties. The stricter wildland–urban interface version (SILVIS 2020) marks 11,045 blocks instead of 38,455 (sensitivity table).
  • Aggregates only. The page shows hexagon, county and state counts; no building or block outlines are published.
  • Microsoft US Building Footprints v2 (ODbL), cap_end mostly 2014–21.
  • Area filter ≥ 40 m² (p19b) vs record points of any size; blocks are whole national components, not clipped to a fire's reach, so the map is lenient by design.
  • Line 89 as stated; definition a0 re-estimates 59–93 across records and eligibility (p28_predictor_link.csv).
  • NLCD 2019 classes 41/42/43/52/71/90/95, 9×9 ≥ 50 %; distances exact to 5 km.
How this panel was checked
  • Every limit listed here is also stated on the panel it affects.
